title: Bangkok Clothes Shopping: How the Markets and Malls Work
seo_title: Bangkok Clothes Shopping: A Real Guide | Oops, Mine Co.
meta_description: Bangkok clothes shopping, plainly: how markets and malls differ, why sizing runs small, which fabrics survive the heat, and how to ask for a better price.
excerpt: Markets or malls, sizing that runs small, fabric that survives the heat, and how to ask for a better price — a plain guide to buying clothes in Bangkok.

hero.intro: Two kinds of shopping happen in Bangkok, and they play by opposite rules. Markets move fast, cost less and hand you no fitting room. Malls hand you a mirror and a fixed price. Here's how both work, what a size really means on a Thai tag, and what to pack.

sections.heading: Bangkok clothes shopping happens at two speeds
paragraphs: Bangkok sells clothes two ways, and the trip goes better once you know which one you're standing in. There are the markets: stalls under awnings, racks that change from week to week, cash, and usually nowhere to try anything on. Then there are the malls: cold air, price tags nobody argues with, card readers, and a mirror you can stand in front of all afternoon. Neither is better. They're separate games with separate rules, and most people who come home happy played both — a market early, while the air is still kind, and a mall in the afternoon when it isn't.

One honest note first. You'll find no addresses, no opening times and no prices here, because those move, and a stale detail sends you across town to a shuttered door. Anyone who has typed bangkok thailand clothes into a search bar has already met the out-of-date version of this advice, so check a place's own site or a current map the morning you go. What doesn't move is how the two kinds of shopping behave, what a number on a Thai label means, which fabrics live through the heat, and how to ask for a better price without souring the exchange.

sections.heading: Markets: where the racks change every week
paragraphs: The names you'll hear most are Chatuchak, a weekend market by name and enormous by any measure, with clothing as one district inside it, and Pratunam, an area built around wholesale clothing where sellers buy by the armful and single pieces are usually still welcome. What they share is turnover: the rack you liked on Saturday may be a different rack next month. That's the charm and also the catch. If you see the one, buy the one — there's rarely a second visit that ends well.

Shop them with a small kit. Small bills, because change for a big one is a chore for everybody. A soft tape measure, because there's often nowhere to try a piece on. A tote, because your hands fill up fast. Go early for cooler air and thinner crowds. Before you pay, run the zip up and down, pull gently at a seam, and turn the garment inside out: Bangkok clothes are cut for the weather they're sold in, so a heavy lining is a sign the piece was made for somebody else's climate.

Shopping from home instead? The tape still decides it. Our size guide shows which numbers to take and how to compare them, so you can lay a dress you already wear on the bed and read the difference. It's the same check you'd run at a stall with the garment in your hands, minus the crowd, the heat and the guessing.
bullets: Small bills for stalls, a card for the malls.
A soft tape measure and your own measurements written down.
A tote you can fold flat, then fill.
Early hours: kinder air, fewer elbows, patient sellers.
Zip, seam, lining — check all three before the money moves.

sections.heading: Malls: fitting rooms, fixed prices and Bangkok Fashion Island
paragraphs: Malls run on the opposite rules. Prices are printed and stay printed, cards work, there are fitting rooms and staff who'll bring you another size, and each shop sets its own exchange terms — ask at the counter and keep the receipt. Several of the big central malls sit along the Skytrain line, which makes an afternoon of them easy to string together. What a mall gives you is consistency: labels hold their sizing across a season, finishing is steadier, and the Thai brands with their own shops are often where the least ordinary pieces are, cut with more thought and priced above a market stall.

Others serve their own neighborhoods further out. Fashion Island lists its address on Thanon Ram Intra in the Khan Na Yao district, well away from the downtown shopping strip, so treat it as its own outing rather than a detour: check the hours on its own site before you set out, and give it the afternoon instead of the hour between two other stops. What you give up in any mall is the hunt — and the hunt is our job, which is what the Thai edit comes of.

sections.heading: Sizing runs small, and "free size" is a real size
paragraphs: Write your measurements on your phone before you fly: bust, waist, hip, and shoulder-to-hem on a dress you already love. Sizing across much of Asia runs smaller than a US label, and the gap is uneven from shop to shop — one seller's medium is another's large. "Free size" means one cut for everyone, which fits a narrow band of bodies beautifully and the rest of us loosely or not at all. Measure it flat, double the width across the chest, and believe the tape over the tag.

That habit follows you home. Our listings carry flat measurements where we have them, not just a size letter, and our size guide shows how we take them, so you can lay a dress you own on the bed and compare. Sitting between two sizes? Send your numbers through the contact page and we'll tell you which one we'd put in the box. Returns come back as store credit on anything postmarked within seven days, with a $15 restocking fee — the returns page has the full terms.

sections.heading: Fabric is the decision the heat makes for you
paragraphs: It's hot and humid in Bangkok for most of the year, and that edits your wardrobe within an hour of landing. Cotton, cotton blends, rayon and viscose, light linen blends, and real Thai silk for an evening all behave. Thick polyester and a full lining don't. Turn things inside out before you buy: a lining that stops at the hip, a seam with room to let out, and a hem that lies flat are the marks of something that lasts past the trip.

That fabric habit is most of why Thai pieces wear so well once they're home — light weight, soft drape, color that stays awake in daylight, and detail you don't meet on every rack: embroidery, a cut-out sleeve, a hand-finished trim. The everyday version lives in our Thai edit, and the traditional Thai clothes guide covers the formal side.

sections.heading: Bargaining, without being that person
paragraphs: Bargaining belongs where prices aren't printed: market stalls, street racks, a table of scarves. It has no place in a mall, a department store, or any shop with a tag on the garment. Where it does fit, treat it as a friendly exchange rather than a contest. Smile, ask what the best price is, make one counter, and take the answer you get. Buying two or three pieces from the same stall earns a better number faster than any amount of pushing on one.

A tiny amount to you can be a real margin to the person running the stall, so don't grind over it. And once a price is agreed, it's agreed; walking off after that reads badly. A few words of Thai help, a thank you helps more. There's nothing to haggle over on our side — the price on a listing is the price — but if something about a piece isn't clear before you buy, the contact page reaches a person, Monday through Saturday.

sections.heading: What to pack, and what to leave room for
paragraphs: Dress for two climates, because you'll meet both on the same block: walking heat outside and cold indoor air the moment a door closes behind you. Light layers, sandals you can slip off at a doorway, and something that covers shoulders and knees for temple visits — a scarf does that job and weighs nothing. Then leave room in the bag; everybody goes home heavier than planned. If the rest of the trip needs a plan too, our packing capsule covers the pieces that mix and the one dress that handles a nice dinner.
bullets: A light long-sleeve layer for cold indoor air and covered shoulders.
A scarf: shoulder cover, wrap, and a new neckline in photos.
Sandals you can step out of, plus a spare pair for a wet afternoon.
A folding tote, and honest space left in the suitcase.
Your measurements, the tape, and a little patience.

We find them — small studios and boutiques in Thailand, along with Korea, Vietnam and elsewhere in Asia — and we carry only what we'd wear ourselves, in runs small enough that you're unlikely to meet your own outfit across a room. faqs.q: Where should I start shopping for clothes in Bangkok?
faqs.a: One market morning and one mall afternoon, then judge the rest of the trip from there. The market shows you what's being made and worn right now; the mall shows you what a label costs with a fitting room attached. Carry a tape measure, small bills and a tote, go early while the air is bearable, and check any place's own site for current hours before you cross the city.

faqs.q: Are the markets cheaper than the malls?
faqs.a: Usually, and you pay for it other ways: no fitting room, no exchange, and a rack that won't be there next week. A mall costs more and hands you a mirror, a printed price and a receipt. We wouldn't decide on price alone — decide on how sure you want to be about the fit. For a piece you plan to wear often, the fitting room tends to win.

faqs.q: Do Thai clothing sizes run small?
faqs.a: Usually, by a size or two against a US label, and it moves from shop to shop, so treat the letter on the tag as an opinion. Measure the garment flat, double the width across chest and hip, and compare it with something at home that fits you well. "Free size" is a real cut rather than a courtesy: it suits a narrow band of bodies and hangs loose on the rest.

No. It fits market stalls and street racks where nothing is priced. In malls, department stores and any shop with a tag on the garment, the price is the price. Where bargaining does belong, keep it light: ask for the best price, make one counter, and accept the answer. Buying two or three pieces together does more for you than pushing hard on one.

faqs.q: Can I buy this kind of thing without flying to Thailand?
faqs.a: That's the whole reason the shop exists. Our Thai edit carries the Thai pieces, and the wider Asian edit adds Korea and elsewhere. Where we have a piece's flat measurements they're on the listing, and the size guide explains how we take them. Returns are store credit on anything postmarked within seven days, and some pieces are final sale — the returns page has the terms.
